title: Map of the Three Volumes of The Feynman Lectures on Physics
text: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, given at Caltech in 1961-63, are three volumes: Volume I is mechanics, radiation, and heat; Volume II is electromagnetism; Volume III is quantum mechanics.

support.source: FLP, preface to the published lectures

title: Volume I, Chapter 1: Atoms in Motion
text: The atomic hypothesis is the sentence Feynman would save if all science were lost: everything is made of atoms, little particles in perpetual motion, attracting when slightly separated and repelling when squeezed together. Temperature, pressure, evaporation, and diffusion are what that jiggling looks like in bulk.

support.quote: all things are made of atoms — little particles that move around in perpetual motion, attracting each other when they are a little distance apart, but repelling upon being squeezed into one another

title: Volume I, Chapter 4: Conservation of Energy
text: Energy is a number that stays the same if you keep every form on the books. It changes costume — motion, heat, height, spring, chemical — and a missing term means the boundary was drawn too small, not that the law failed.

title: Volume I, Chapter 6: Probability and Random Walks
text: A probability is a count of how often something happens in a long series of trials, not a mood. A random walk is the same idea: each step is uncertain, and the spread of many steps grows like the square root of the number of steps.

title: Volume I, Chapter 7: Gravitation
text: The same inverse-square attraction that pulls an apple also holds the Moon and the planets. Newton’s law is one rule for both, and the orbit is just the fall that never hits the ground.

title: Volume I, Chapter 9: Newtonian Dynamics
text: F=ma is the special case of a deeper rule: force is the rate of change of momentum. When the mass is constant the two statements agree; when mass changes, as in a rocket, you have to keep the momentum form.

title: Volume I, Chapters 15 and 16: Special Relativity and Energy-Momentum
text: Special relativity starts from the fact that the speed of light is the same for every inertial observer, not from objects mysteriously shrinking. From that, time and the energy-momentum relation follow, with the rest energy mc² sitting in the formula even when the particle is still.

title: Volume I, Chapter 44: The Laws of Thermodynamics and Entropy
text: Entropy is a state function. For a reversible path it changes by the heat added divided by the temperature, and it counts how many microscopic arrangements fit the same macroscopic description.

title: Volume I, Chapter 46: Ratchet, Irreversibility, and Thermal Fluctuations
text: A ratchet and pawl look as if they could turn random molecular kicks into one-way work. They cannot, if the whole machine sits in one heat bath: the pawl jiggles too, and the machine runs backward as often as forward.

title: Volume I, Chapters 47 to 49: Waves, Beats, and Normal Modes
text: A wave hands a local shake to the next bit of the medium. Two tones close in frequency beat: the amplitude swells and fades at the difference frequency. A complicated motion can be taken apart into normal modes, each ringing at its own frequency.

title: Volume I, Chapter 49: Normal Modes, Pitch, and Loudness
text: Hit a mode harder and, to a good approximation, you raise the amplitude, which the ear hears as louder, not as a higher pitch. Pitch is the frequency of the mode. A very hard hit can bring in other modes and change the sound, but the note of a given mode does not climb just because it is louder.

title: Volume II, Chapter 1: Electromagnetic Interactions
text: The electric force between the charges in ordinary matter is enormous. Matter stays neutral because plus and minus cancel almost perfectly; the leftover unbalanced piece is what we notice as electricity, chemistry, and the stiffness of solids.

title: Volume II, Chapter 4: The Electrostatic Field and Gauss's Law
text: In electrostatics the field is fixed by the charges and by the boundary. Gauss’s law says the flux of E through a closed surface is the charge inside divided by ε0, which is often the shortest way to find the field when the symmetry is kind.

title: Volume II, Chapter 17: Electromagnetic Induction
text: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit drives an electric field around the circuit. The induced emf is minus the rate of change of that flux. Moving a wire in a steady field and changing the field through a still wire are two ways of seeing the same law.

title: Volume II, Chapter 18: Maxwell's Equations and Light
text: Maxwell’s equations tie charge, current, E, and B into one system. A changing electric field acts as a current, and the coupled fields propagate as light at the speed c = 1/√(ε0μ0).

title: Volume II, Chapter 19: The Principle of Least Action
text: The true path is the one for which a small wiggle does not change the action to first order. The action is stationary. Newton’s laws and the optical rule of least time are both special cases of that statement.

title: Volume III, Chapter 1: Quantum Behavior and the Double Slit
text: A quantum object is not a little billiard ball and not a classical wave. In the double-slit experiment the probability shows interference when both paths are open, and the interference disappears if the experiment tells which slit was used.

title: Volume III, Chapter 3: Combining Probability Amplitudes
text: If you cannot tell the alternatives apart, you add the amplitudes and then square. If the alternatives are distinguishable, you add the probabilities. That is the whole difference between interference and an ordinary mixture.

title: Volume III, Chapters 8 to 10: Two-State Systems and the Hamiltonian Matrix
text: A great many quantum problems can be cut down to two base states and the amplitude for jumping between them. The Hamiltonian matrix is just the table of those energies and couplings, and the time dependence follows from it.

title: Volume III, Chapter 17: Symmetry and Conservation Laws
text: A symmetry means the predictions do not change when you change the description in a certain way. Each such indifference is tied to a conservation law: shift in space to momentum, shift in time to energy, rotation to angular momentum.
